subtitle: A duel decided by one opening

body: Bushido Blade is Lightweight's 1997 PlayStation fighting game about armed duels, first released in Japan on 14 March. A sword strike can end the encounter immediately, making a small error more important than a long sequence of successful attacks. Six fighters and eight weapons offer different combinations of speed, reach and strength. The absence of a health bar changes the rhythm of watching an opponent: every approach could become the final exchange. Waiting, retreating and choosing a stance become as meaningful as the moment a weapon finally moves.

A blow can wound without killing. Damage to an arm may remove two-handed attacks or the ability to throw a secondary weapon; injured legs can leave a fighter crawling. The Body Damage System therefore changes the actions available during the duel instead of simply subtracting a number. High, neutral and low stances provide different attacks, while the Motion Shift System connects one swing to another. A successful defence preserves more than life: it keeps movement and weapons available for the next attempt to find a vulnerable angle.

The fighters can run, jump and climb through connected parts of a castle compound, including a grove, moat and maze of bridges. Combat can move beyond the small space where it began. A katana, rapier or naginata makes distance useful in a different way, so choosing where to stand is part of choosing how to fight. Bushido Blade attracted attention for this unusual treatment of damage and freedom of movement. A direct sequel followed on PlayStation in 1998, continuing an alternative to the round-based exchanges familiar from contemporary fighting games.
